# Cultural values in disaster discourse: Behavioral propositions from the Philippines

Jose Enrique Ramirez , Nymphmary Daphne Santiago , Terese E. Venus

Bioeconomy Economics Research Group, University of Passau, Germany

## A R T I C L E I N F O

Keywords: Resilience Typhoon Philippines Adaptation Discourse analysis Qualitative

## A B S T R A C T

Cultural value systems represent important behavioral channels in determining how individuals and institutions manage climate disasters. This is particularly relevant in the Philippines, where disasters are so frequent, they are considered part of daily life. Drawing on this perspective, we examine how cultural value systems manifest in post-disaster discourses following major typhoons. We conduct a discourse analysis using social media comments after four major typhoons from 2013 to 2021. We propose six behavioral propositions related to how culture affects responses to climate disasters in the Philippines: (i) supernatural explanations as a basis for interpreting climatic events, (ii) self-reliance as a justification for limited institutional engagement in adaptation, (iii) the effect of low trust in authority on negative perceptions towards taxation and preferences for community-based responses, (iv) the preference to donate to directly to recipients, including a hierarchy of acceptable intermediaries, (v) the view of prayer as an effective and cost-efficient non-material form of aid, and (vi) the perception of discourse as a detraction from the immediate need to help. We recommend that future studies and behavioral interventions consider these cultural value systems in disaster-related decision-making in the Philippines.

## 1. Introduction

Extreme weather events have been occurring more frequently and with greater intensity globally [1]. The Philippines represents one of the most vulnerable countries given its location within the Pacific Ring of Fire [2,3]. In 2022, it experienced 232 extreme weather events and disasters, and 82 of them were meteorological (i.e., typhoons and monsoons) [4]. Currently, 74% of its population is at risk, over $^ { 7 0 , 0 0 0 }$ related deaths have occurred since 1990 [5], and the country experiences an average annual asset loss of \$3.5 billion in damages [6].

Some of the biggest disasters have been typhoons: Typhoon Haiyan (Yolanda) struck in 2013 and has been widely regarded as the deadliest and costliest typhoon in the country's history. It resulted in over 16 million affected persons, 6300 deaths, 1062 missing persons, and over 1.1 million destructed houses, all accounting for \$2.2 billion in damages [7]. In 2018, Typhoon Mangkhut (Ompong) led to 127 deaths [8]. In 2021, Typhoon Rai (Odette) was the country's second costliest typhoon at \$1.02 billion (National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management, 2022), impacting both the Visayas and Mindanao regions with a death toll of 407 [9]. In 2020, Typhoon Goni (Rolly) and Typhoon Vamco (Ulysses) occurred within a week of each other and demonstrated the phenomenon of compounding disasters. Goni was the world's strongest typhoon of 2020 [10], while Vamco was the country's deadliest and costliest typhoon of that year, resulting in 102 deaths and \$418 million in damages [11].

Given the frequency of disasters, they are often considered accepted occurences in daily life and deeply intertwined with Filipino culture [12]. For this reason, previous literature has investigated the role of culture and local knowledge in disaster recovery and adaptation efforts [13–19]. Social vulnerability has also been found to contribute to the spatial variability in risk related to disasters [20]. While these studies largely conclude that a culturally-sensitive approach is needed to understand post-disaster needs and vulnerabilities [15], the majority of these studies focus on singular disasters using field research. Our study builds on this approach by analyzing the discourse around several disasters, which offers a comparative perspective on post-disaster responses. We contribute to disaster research by showing how cultural value systems operate and may affect public reasoning about climate disasters. By synthesizing the discourse across four major typhoons, we identify six propositions that explain how value-driven interpretations influence perceptions of responsibility, institutional trust, and preferred modes of disaster response. In doing so, we demonstrate that cultural value systems systematically structure public expectations in ways that help generate hypotheses about why certain behavioral responses will be more effective in Philippine disaster governance.

## 2. Conceptual framework: Culture and disaster discourses

Cultural values affect how people perceive and respond to climate disasters in both their immediate reactions and long-term economic behavior. One important aspect of this process, for example, is disaster framing, which is determined by underlying beliefs, traditions and social norms and in turn, affects the emerging narratives and responses. Previous research has highlighted the role of indigenous knowledge and intangible cultural heritage in disaster discourse, particular in the improvement of early warning systems and adaptation [18].

We begin with the concept of cultural value systems, which can be understood as the broader set of values, beliefs, and narratives [21]. While such cultural systems provide an interpretive background, not all cultural elements have direct implications on behavior. Then, we argue that cultural value systems become shared rules, expectations, and interpretive frameworks, when they are collectively stabilized and translated into socially shared expectations or normative beliefs. As North [22] describes, they include “sanctions, taboos, customs, traditions, conventions, codes of conduct and norms of behavior”, which are enforced by peers and others who impose costs on the individual who does not uphold them [21]. In our case, these cultural values affect how people understand climate disasters and what responses they consider legitimate or appropriate.

These cultural values can be observed in concrete discursive practices, including how extreme events are named, interpreted, and narrated in public discourse. Similarly, disaster framing can also be represented in the naming of events. For example, different naming of the 2013 Philippine super typhoon as Haiyan (international name) or Yolanda (Filipino name) created different narratives. Haiyan was discussed through a scientific and Western globalized lens of “climate change, freak storms, and (the corresponding) poverty”, which focused on response through adaptation measures [23]. In contrast, Yolanda emphasized the social narratives of “national politics, accusations of incompetence, and identity” underscored by “a strong sense of self-blame and unworthiness that views the typhoon and its aftermath as God's punishment for people's kumpyansa, or overconfidence, and their lack of belief”, which was described as a passivity in response to disaster [23].

This so-called “passivity” is further reinforced by other cultural beliefs that influence disaster response. For example, religious values are often involved in decision-making about disaster evacuations, as many participants had claimed that non-evacuation is divine test of faith [24]. Similarly, Bankoff [12] described how community members in Tarlac chose not to evacuate from the mudflows of the Mount Pinatubo eruption in 1991 and placed religious statues in front of their homes hoping that faith could divert the mudflows elsewhere. These beliefs represent the Filipino value of “bahala na” (fatalistic risk-taking) and demonstrate how certain values may sometimes lead to inaction, which in turn affect long-term disaster response patterns.

Increasing climate disasters has also impacted cultural and religious institutions' perceptions of themselves. Cornelio and Teehankee [25] note that the rise in global religious philanthropy, through faith-based or religious organizations, comes from the notion that “disaster response opens up the opportunity for religion to assert itself as a social institution of relevance in global society” through giving as an extension of their religious doctrine. However, they also note a paradox that their increased prominence can also be acts of power with the disaster response being a potential space for increasing a group's social capital [25].

Frequent disasters mean that Filipinos may already be jaded from disaster as an everyday reality [12,14]. For example, participants decided not to evacuate during Typhoon Haiyan because typhoons are regular occurrences and many believed that Haiyan would be a typical storm [24]. This translates to donation behavior. While it is intuitive that direct victims of disasters have fewer financial resources to donate, previous research suggests that their lower charitable giving is not due only to economic hardship. For example, Berrebi, Karlinsky, and Yonah [26] find that charitable giving is less common among the actual victim groups as compared to neighboring and distant communities in the United States. Yet, they also discover that every additional disaster leads to decreased instances of charitable giving, which may imply that compounding disasters influence the presence of disaster fatigue. Ressler, Paxton, and Velasco [27] note that United States non-profits’ embeddedness in a community (i.e. aligning religious identity, geographic proximity, and strong social networks) increases donations.

Studies about economic behavior in humanitarian contexts in the Philippines is limited. In the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, Palanca-Tan and Tan [28] found that purely altruistic Filipino donations to food banks are less frequent than intended egoistic donations to vaccination programs, where they would also benefit from them. Kurata, Prasetyo, Ong, Cahigas et al. [29,30] found that is that having a higher understanding of Typhoon Rai (Odette) in 2021 led to a perception of high vulnerability and severity, which leads to a positive intention to donate. They also claim that intentions to donate come from one's behavioral control over social pressures, such as the media [29,30]. Among American participants' attitudes to donating to Typhoon Haiyan, Manesi, van Lange, van Doesum, and Pollet [31] found that social values orientation, social mindfulness, educational attainment, and political leaning were predictive of donation behavior.

Social media adds another dimension to disaster response and economic behavior. Liu and Xu [32] analyze three disasters and note that while the public uses it as a means to discuss response options, social media can increase situational awareness and reinforce gratitude to disaster managers. However, social media can also lead to misinformation [33] and data overload (Palen & Hughes). In the context of pro-social behavior, Okada, Ishida, and Yamauchi [34], in the aftermath of the 2011 Japan earthquake, note that initiatives with social media platforms were seen to have more effective donation solicitation efforts than those who set up a platform afterward. This suggests that social media can help to facilitate immediate response after disasters and facilitate long-term financial support.

Much of the literature on social media in the Philippines' disaster context almost exclusively discusses Typhoon Haiyan. Takahashi, Tandoc, and Carmichael [35] found that users' main behaviors during Haiyan were to “disseminate second-hand information, memorialize those affected, and coordinate relief efforts.” Similarly, Tandoc and Takahashi [36] found an emotional element for those directly affected that social media became an outlet of “collective coping amid the breakdown of traditional media platforms.” They note that users in Tacloban used social media to communicate their survival status, assess the state of relief efforts, and find emotional. Similarly, David, Ong, and Legara [37] describe the evolution of social media discourse after the disaster. The first few days of the disaster focused on informational content, while the succeeding days shifted to disaster relief stories, political commentaries of foreign response, and aid mobilization. This maintained (inter)national attention and broadened the potential donor pool. This aligns with Soriano, Roldan, Cheng, and Oco [38]'s finding that expressing solidarity, engaging in debate, and sharing volunteer and donation works see social media as a platform for “acts of civil engagement.” Subsequently, McKay and Perez [39] highlight how citizen aid groups can attain a “moral capital” in humanitarian work over government actors. In particular, showcasing “local knowledge, perceived responsiveness, and transparency” through selected imagery as a communication medium builds legitimacy and increases trust among both donors and beneficiaries [39].

In addition to the culturally grounded perspectives, disaster discourse can be embedded within the broader traditions of discourse analysis. From a Foucaultian perspective of the order of discourse, discursive practices are typically analyzed with a four-step critique: (i) who is excluded or silenced, (ii) what internal rules regulate what it is said, (iii) what historical and institutional conditions make these statements possible and (iv) how discourses circular reflect and reproduce power relations [40,41]. While we do not apply a strictly Foucauldian analysis, this perspective is reflected through our analysis of how disaster related discourses define who is authorized to speak, what interpretative frames are privileged and how cultural values intersect with institutional conditions. Similarly, we draw upon Fairclough's critical discourse analysis, which views how public text mix storylines and formats drive social change [42]. While the posts mix familiar storylines and formats, disaster narratives can make some responses (e.g. resilience) feel natural while sidelining others (e.g. institutional reform). Further, we consider framing analysis, which defines four core functions of frames: problem definition, casual attribution, moral evaluation and treatment recommendation [43]. In our study, this is useful for understanding how discourses of disaster are constructed and contested.

## 3. Methodology

In this study, we conduct a discourse analysis of social media comments after four major typhoons from 2013 to 2021. Our methodological and analytical considerations are informed by Sikolohiyang Pilipino (“Filipino Psychology”).

## 3.1. Discourse analysis

This study follows a discourse analysis methodology, which is situated in both cultural grounded and embedded in traditions of discourse analysis. Our discourse analysis, defined by Taylor [44] as “the close study of language and language use as evidence of aspects of society and social life,” is consistent with Filipino Psychology's aspirations for uncovering values and realities in a socially constructed manner. Its main methodological consideration is to analyze textual meanings while simultaneously considering their discursive contexts, that is the meanings that arise out of interrelated discourses [45]. This entails a strong degree of reflexivity and interpretation on the researcher's part, as interpretation may be highly subjective.

This study utilizes the Filipino Psychology (Sikolohiyang Pilipino) approach to guide its methodological and analytical considerations [46,47]. Its form of academic protest comes from the perceived disenfranchisement felt by the adaptation of Western psychological concepts as a universal psychology, which determines Filipinos' identity and creates a “struggle for a national cultural identity” [46,48]. It then acts as a “responsible psychology” due to its desire to be responsive to serving Filipino interests in multiple disciplines [47–49]. It prioritizes emic and inductive approaches that spotlight pakikiramdam, a form of indirect communication through a “shared inner perception” that practices “feeling for another”, being privy to social cues, contexts, and empathy toward one's research partners. In turn, this influences the development of localized research methods involving culturally sensitive forms of questioning, community immersion, and rapport building. This bottom-up focus and inclination for multi-method triangulation reinforces an “indigenization from within” that emphasizes using the experiences, ideas, and cultural orientation of the Filipinos as the basis for hypothesis creation [48,50].

Within the framework of Filipino Psychology, we operationalize several core Filipino cultural values frequently referenced in post-disaster discourse. Three core values are explicitly included within the framework and include kapwa (shared identity), bahala na (fatalistic risk-taking) and utang na loob (debt of gratitude). In addition to these, we include bayanihan (collective cooperation) and diskarte (being strategic) due to their relevance in the context of disaster response (Table 1). Appendix 2 provides the full list of cultural value definitions.

To integrate these epistemological commitments with systematic analytical procedures, we apply a directed qualitative content analysis approach. Directed content analysis begins with an existing theoretical framework (i.e. the set of core Filipino cultural value) and uses empirical data to validate, refine, and extend it. These values are also referenced explicitly or implicitly in our analysis of social media comments, which indicates they are analytically relevant for interpreting post-disaster discourse. To avoid treating these concepts as self-evident, we operationalize them as described in the following paragraphs.

The kapwa is a “recognition of shared identity, an inner self shared with others” [50]. It mediates human interactions by treating others as “fellow” human beings, which connotes a degree of respect and treating “others” as part of oneself. It follows that each interaction has a corresponding level of “sharedness” with another [48]. Kapwa is also seen as the core of the value structures brought about by Sikolohiyang Pilipino, ranging from “surface values” to “interpersonal values.”

A religiously rooted value is bahala na, which translates to “leave it to God” or “God-willing”. It is a common saying that often takes on different connotations depending on the tone and conversation context. It represents that there is uncertainty in the future, but hope that divine intervention will take care of it [51]. It represents both resignation and fatalism coupled with hope [52]. In disaster applications, it entails a specific form of risk-taking [47] through various scenarios such as deciding whether to evacuate or stay home [14], praying as a mitigation strategy [12], or reasoning with inhumane post-disaster consequences (i.e. forced relocation and lack of services) as a means to wider salvation [13]. In the Philippines, the primary religion is Roman Catholicism, as 78.8% of Filipinos identify with the religion (Gregorio, 2023). It is important to note that while religious and fatalistic interpretations recur frequently in documented discourse, they represent only one of several interpretive frames and should not be taken as universal characteristics of Filipino culture.

Utang na loob is another prominent value, which approximately translates to “debt of gratitude”. It is an obligation to reciprocate as a form of showing gratefulness for a deed towards a person, which oftentimes creating a mix of helplessness and embarrassment to ask for more when one has not yet paid their dues [53].

One value not discussed within the framework, but notable in the context of Filipino disaster response is bayanihan, which approximately translates to “collective cooperation”. It is a word used by many disaster stakeholders in promoting community-based assistance and recovery. It originates as “the ancient Filipino custom of group work” creating “a system of mutual help and concern which has become the backbone of family and village life through the Philippines” (Ang, 1979). The word has consistently been used among (inter)national leaders and NGOs as a commendable term to represent this form of support, particularly during the post-Typhoon Haiyan [54] and COVID-19 responses (to which the law that declared a national health emergency was “Bayanihan to Heal as One Act”). However, criticisms remain that it “romanticizes an indigenous coping strategy” and “evades government responsibility” [54].

Additionally, we analyze the value of diskarte, which loosely translates to “being strategic” [55]. Previous research has noted that the concept is central to the Filipino identity and represents an essential set of skills needed to survive [56].

## 3.2. Data collection and analysis

We use textual analysis from social media comments. We gather online sentiments due to their wide availability and accessibility to potentially be representative of the general population, as the country is persistently highly placed in social media usage rankings. Specifically, the Philippines had 80.3 million Facebook users in 2023, which accounts for 69% of the country's population and 93.5% of all eligible users [57]. For this reason, we selected Facebook as a social media platform to analyze discourse. Notably, we do not view Facebook as a neutral repository of opinions, but as a discursive environment in which content is created and manipulated based on platform-specific characteristics and interactions. Specifically, there are algorithms that determine the visibility and circulation of posts that may amplify certain narratives. This has been documented, for example, through experimental evidence on Facebook's algorithms, which reduce exposure to content with different views [58]. As a result, the discourses analyzed in this study should be understood as emerging from these platform-mediated dynamics, which affect how cultural value systems are articulated and reproduced.

The textual analysis from social media comments functions as the study's primary method. These comments are taken within the discursive context of four major typhoon disasters within the last 11 years: Typhoon Haiyan (Yolanda) in 2013, Typhoon Goni (Rolly) in 2020, Typhoon Vamco (Ulysses) in 2020, and Typhoon Rai (Odette) in 2021. We selected these events due to their prominence in the Filipinos' way of life. Bankoff [12] highlights how they live with “normalized threat” due to these typhoons' frequency. Moreover, typhoons' relative ease of prediction and slow onset means that preparation activities can more easily be accounted for. While earthquakes are frequent, they are difficult to prepare for on an individual level. While volcanic eruptions may also occur (such as the Taal Volcano eruption of 2020), their infrequency makes this specific kind of threat not “normalized”. Further, there are specific dynamics based on the time frame in which these disasters occurred. Beyond the disasters happening from 2013 to 2021 helping the method's social media nature, the study observes the change in the time between Haiyan, the country's most consequential typhoon in history, with three typhoons occurring seven to eight years later. Moreover, the study also observes the potential evolutionary dynamics between compounding typhoons Goni and Vamco, which occurred within a week of each other, and the discourses on the latter three accounting for other social factors (i.e., responses to the COVID-19 pandemic and 2020 Taal Volcano eruption).

Based on these events, we evaluate the existing discourses on disaster response and relief through the comments sections of various posts referring to news articles, social commentaries, donation calls, impactful visuals, and state and non-state statements. The posts yielded more than 37,500 comments across the four typhoons. From this larger pool, we systematically screened comments using explicit inclusion criteria: they had to be relevant to Filipino cultural values, show engagement (e.g., reactions or replies), and contribute substantively to the discourse rather than being spam, single-word responses, or duplicates. After this screening process, 306 comments remained for close discourse analysis. We selected the posts based on a combination of keywords acting as search terms using Facebook's search function (Appendix 1). All posts under one search term were screened for potential usage in the study until Facebook's search function stopped loading posts. In terms of ethical considerations, all posts analyzed in this study were publicly accessible. Further, we followed established ethical guidelines for social media research. All comments were fully anonymized, and no personal data, profile information, or metadata were collected or stored. The posts included in the Appendix have been translated to English from their original Tagalog, which would make back-searching nearly impossible. Posts must have reached a threshold of either 200 reactions or 100 comments to represent “dominant discourses.” From these posts, the inclusion criteria were that the comments were appropriate, applicable to the Filipino values of interest and that each comment had additional engagements (e.g.

Diagram 1. Overview of the methodological process.

reactions or comment replies to identify points of (dis)agreement and discussion). This purposive approach follows qualitative standards that prioritize discursive salience over volume. We determined that theoretical saturation was reached when no new values or discursive frames emerged in later coding rounds, and importantly, the same cultural themes (resilience, prayer, bayanihan, distrust in institutions, supernatural framing) consistently recurred across disasters.

The posts were stored in a database and analyze each post on a dedicated spreadsheet (Appendices 3 and 4, respectively). We provide a specific interpretation of each selected comment based on Filipino values and the comment's contribution to the discourse. However, these quotations presented in the results are used illustratively to exemplify broader patterns identified across the dataset rather than as singular evidence for specific claims.

In line with Gill's [59] two phases to analyzing discourse, all interpretations were gathered and clustered into 13 comment patterns that reflect the most prominent discourses within the four events. These comment patterns do not represent a side in a particular argument but are rather focused on “variability (differences within and between accounts) and consistency”. These “features of the discourse” within the comment patterns then helped form six central preliminary propositions. Each proposition consists of selecting insights from one to four comment patterns, with the potential to overlap for further depth. This process is exemplified in Appendix 5. Diagram 1 presents a visual representation of the data collection and analysis process.

All coding was conducted by the first author, whose background is in sociology and has a deep familiarity with Philippine culture and language. We acknowledge that this positionality may have affected the interpretation of the discourses. As recent methodological work has found, positionality can also enhance the reflexivity and transparency in qualitative analysis by making the researcher more conscious of interpretative choices [60]. Within our framework of Filipino Psychology, there is an emphasis on culturally grounded, emic perspectives. This aligns closely with the reflexive recognition of the researcher's standpoint in coding.

## 4. Results

Given the strict enforcement of the 200 reactions or 100 comments engagement threshold, the study accounted for 46 Facebook posts taken within the discourses of the four disasters, with most being sourced from news outlets due to their role as a centralized platform with high discourse concentration. Subsequently, “resilience” was the most common search term among the selected posts for the same reason, as posts containing specific acts or actors did not yield high engagement. The breakdown of the selected posts include:

• 15 posts concerned Typhoon Haiyan, with a total of 5472 comments

• Three posts concerned Typhoon Goni, with a total of 6500 comments

• Five posts concerned Typhoon Vamco, with a total of 4188 comments

• 12 posts concerned both Goni and Vamco due to its consecutive nature, with a total of 2427 comments

• 11 posts concerned Typhoon Rai, with a total of 18,986 comments

While these posts contained over 37,500 comments, not all were made accessible due to potential factors such as spam comments, deactivated accounts, and Facebook's limitation of not enabling us to view all comments. Moreover, not all available comments were pre-screened due to the indicated requirements of a comment requiring a form of additional engagement and substantive content devoid of spam, single-word responses, or duplicates. Based on all the aforementioned inclusion criteria, a total of 306 pre-screened comments were chosen for individual interpretation.

It is important to note that overlapping themes emerged within the comments during the categorization process, as one comment could have been relevant for more than one of the propositions. More specifically, while 306 pre-screened comments were selected for interpretation, 387 data points informed the propositions due to some comments intersecting with the developed themes.

Overall, six central preliminary propositions were identified with respect to Filipino Psychology (Table 2). Across the four disasters, we find that cultural values consistently structure discourses about responsibility, appropriate action, and institutional performance. The six propositions below reflect how these informal institutions influence disaster reasoning across events.

## 4.1. Climate disaster perceptions

Proposition #1: The discourse surrounding climate disasters often frames them as inevitable and supernatural phenomena rather than the direct result of human-induced environmental degradation.

This proposition highlights the discourse that disasters are widely viewed as an inevitable phenomenon due to the Philippines geographical position. The comments demonstrate an acceptance and resignation to this situation, with posts attempting to find refuge by noting that the country is lucky that it has not experienced the “worst” circumstances relative to other disasters or other immediate needs (i.e., hunger, violence, etc.) while also claiming that disasters impacts are amplified as part of a vicious cycle with the country's persistent poverty and corruption.

Most of the discourse concerning disasters’ root causes gravitated toward supernatural justifications. Its most prominent theme focuses on how Filipinos view the role of religion in disasters com.

An example of religion's role in contextualizing disasters is through how Filipinos attempt to match their disaster lived experience with their understanding of Catholic doctrine, particularly with stories from the Holy Bible. One discourse, particularly about posts with striking visuals of flooding and its resulting damages, illustrates that climate disasters occur similarly with scriptures such as The Great Flood and the Lord's Prayer in reference to the apocalyptic-like tests whereby God decides who deserves heaven and hell (comment 3M).

Despite their increasing strength, climate disasters are viewed favorably because God is using His attention toward the Philippines. Various lines, including “strong through trials” (comment 16A) and “we are God's children” (comment 20B) point to disasters even being more encouraged because of their parallels with the story being tested and eventually brought to the promised land. Its consequence is in the seemingly thankful and optimistic nature Filipinos feel that their survival from disasters is a sign of God's greater love and preferential treatment for them in relation to others. Living out this fatalistic mindset leads to spiritual healing borne from an acceptance that one's fate is not in their control. In this sense, strengthening and compounding disasters are also viewed positively as proof that consistent survival validates one's belief that they are a “chosen” population (comment 10H)

“I will still thank the Lord, even if I have lost my house and my harvest that my family has been spared” translated from a comment post-Typhoon Rai (comment 43B)

A more pessimistic religious discourse validates the points made by Bankoff [12,14] on Filipinos’ view of calamities as “divine justice” for their wrongdoings. Disasters start to serve as reminders from God to shift values and turn towards Him. The aforementioned human climate actions of logging, poor waste management, and overdevelopment—along with the rise of individual-level crimes (i.e., kidnappings, stealing, drug usage)—are thus treated as acts of selfishness and turning a blind eye to God. Disaster preparation often involves significant amounts of repentance for sins and prayer to increase spiritual wealth and resolve, hoping that enough faith will ensure survival and “true richness” (comment 46D).

The linkage between God and nature was loose, as those who spoke about God solely spoke about nature through Filipinos committing sins and abuses toward “God's creations” comment 37G) Nature, on its own, only comprised a small amount of the existing discourse, with most posts following a similar supernatural argument that disasters are nature's “retaliation” (comment 3K) for overdevelopment. These discourses do not explicitly refer to climate change as an ongoing phenomenon. Instead, they specifically include “mother” in crafting the phrase “mother nature,” an entity with nurturing yet punishing capabilities.

The discourse's proposed interventions, viewed through the lens of nature, involve the standard environmental rehabilitation practices of tree planting, reduced quarrying, and a shift toward more climate-friendly infrastructure. Subsequently, no nature-related points were mentioned on potential mechanisms for surviving disasters. In this regard, most posts highlight nature's wrath and unpredictability as something one can only hope to recover from (comment 44B).

While some of the posts (7 comments) note that climate disasters are consequences of human actions (e.g. poor waste management practices, increased logging, and prioritizing industrialization/overdevelopment, which leads to inadequate flood control infrastructure and can even risk other climate-related disasters, including famines), the majority of such sentiments are from posts originating from climate groups and activists. This group also broadly expresses their grievances that climate change and disasters caused by human error.

The other posts from the non-climate advocacy population (6 comments) acknowledge that while climate change is a reality faced by Filipinos, there are debates on how it translates to disasters’ impact on communities. In particular, they discuss whether the damages are due to humans enabling typhoons to increase strength or their weak infrastructure creating a lower absorptive capacity.

## 4.2. Filipino resilience

Proposition #2: Resilience is often framed as an essential cultural trait among Filipinos in disaster settings, but its frequent invocation risks overshadowing solutions and accountability.

The discourse on resilience frames it as a key Filipino cultural value to maintain optimism and make the most out of hardships. Oftentimes, posts containing people smiling in front of disaster-caused damages would note such persistent positivity as the “true Filipino spirit.” Its embodiment comes in comments telling each other kapit (hold on), to be matatag (stable), and to smile through the pain. It also contains a religious component akin to the previous proposition that maintaining the right attitude will allow God to “provide the rest” (comment 46B).

Filipinos also see resilience as the common-sense direction one should follow in. It is an understanding that life is a constant change and that adapting to such change is the silver lining in ensuring one can still live dignified. Resilience functions as a coping mechanism when confronting climate disasters because it indicates that one still seeks to do something with one's life. Failure to be resilient is seen as a sign of self-deprecation because it asks, “what are you going to do about yourself given the circumstances other than to be strong.” It is a manifestation of pagbabangon (rising again) (comment 25E).

Based on this discourse, Filipino resilience is not one-dimensional but has different layers of meaning. First, it can refer to coping resilience, or the emotional and social capacity to endure hardship through smiling, joking, laughing, remaining hopeful, and continuing to live despite loss. Second, it can refer to religious resilience, where endurance is connected to faith and divine provision. Third, it may also reflect adaptive agency, where resilience is not passive acceptance but a way of adapting and adjusting to circumstances under constrained conditions.

While the definition of Filipino resilience was widely agreed upon, the rest of its discourse became contentious when the discussion shifted toward its political implications, particularly in relation to institutional responsibility for disaster preparedness and response. In this case, its optimistic feature is often framed in discourse as being associated with complacency toward the attitudinal status quo, both on individual and systemic levels.

At the individual level, resilience may encourage people to accept that the circumstances of one's life, and the corresponding suffering, are beyond their control, while simultaneously having full agency in dealing with the consequences. Handling problems solely through resilience becomes a band-aid solution because there is no supposed effort to tackle the root causes of such issues—further highlighting Bankoff's [12,14] point that living in a “permanent emergency” with threat as normalized a part of daily life can make suffering trivial and part of the norm. This is demonstrated by the following comment:

“Filipinos have no choice but to move on. That’s how it always is in the news. A sweetener to hide sour taste!” – translated from a comment post-Typhoons Goni and Vamco (comment 2A)

At the institutional level, the discourse features the two prominent phrases of “romanticizing resilience” and “toxic positivity” (comments 4A and 32B). Both view Filipino resilience as inherently good when speaking of the aforementioned coping mechanism when faced with a life-or-death situation. However, its persistent invocation claims to allow the institutions to utilize resilience as a component of disaster response, which leaves it prone to abuse by diverting resources and lessening interventions that would have otherwise been acted on if the Filipino population had not had a strong willpower and mental fortitude to answer for themselves. Within this discourse, resilience is transformed into a pre-existing cultural asset to shift disaster management to individual-centric responses and coping.

On the other hand, opponents argue that resilience is a decoy for the government to sway a narrative that the present disaster response framework has been successful. Within this narrative, some commenters suggest that such framing may contribute to perceptions that other aspects of disaster response do not need proactive improvements. Much of the discourse also highlights that the existing mechanisms in preparation, mainly through poor infrastructure and temporary housing, will only be addressed until they have proven to fail (i.e., destroyed bridges and washed houses). This sentiment also translates to local governments’ persistent insistence on outdated and climate-unfriendly projects, such as single-use plastics, heavy use of concrete, and tree-cutting (comment 26D).

Another aspect of this discourse presents a more fatalistic interpretation of resilience, viewing it as a value that will be challenging to unlearn because it is inherent in the country's colonial and modern history of struggle. Some claim that demanding accountability is a reality that only some Filipinos can imagine as others have a lack of governance education. Moreover, the Philippine political system is widely considered inefficient, which provides minimal opportunities for citizen feedback and widespread reform (comment 1B).

Finally, a portion of this discourse sees a resignation toward the inverse through embracing resilience and enabling the current setup, as these posters believe that Filipinos require inward accountability to answer for their government because they are the authority to be followed. This is a sign of utang na loob by needing to serve them in return. According to this discourse, efforts made by the government to assist should be acknowledged as an add-on rather than an obligation (comment 24C).

## 4.3. Trust in the government

Proposition #3: Public trust in competent government intervention can influence perceptions of taxation and the extent to which communitybased disaster responses are necessary.

As highlighted in the previous proposition, Filipinos can survive and maintain optimism despite lacking institutional assistance during climate disasters. This sentiment extends to the discussion of appropriate disaster relief and recovery interventions, as the discourses show great disdain for how government actors operate in disasters’ immediate aftermath.

An example is how the distribution of relief packages was delayed due to instances whereby politicians will visit the packing sites for photo opportunities or add an extra step in the assembly process by including their names, photos, or campaign slogans on the relief packs. These occasions would also usually include speeches and often contain “lip service” about “rising up together” (comment 34F) which is another invocation of resilience. While none of the discourses focused explicitly on corruption, many discourses signaled accusations and worries of malpractice due to its historical prevalence in other aspects of Philippine politics (comment 12B, comment 31E).

Most of these sentiments were in response to Typhoon Haiyan. This is strongly related to previous studies about the country's patronage politics, whereby competitive tensions exist at local and national levels but have a mutually reinforcing dynamic of attempting to consolidate power among themselves [61]. For example, a rivalry between the representatives of the national government and the government of Tacloban, a strongly affected area, created a political standoff amid the disaster recovery phase [62]. Similarly, Villaluz [63]'s ethnographic work during Haiyan highlighted “compromised accountability” through a “dichotomy on local or national prerogative”, which claims to have delayed immediate relief from national government funds.

Another point in this discourse is Filipinos’ distrust in how government actors handle foreign aid. This discourse, highlights fears of corruption through leaders pocketing foreign aid:

“Watch the donations! Maybe just a few will go to the victims. We need to publish and broadcast where these were used, how much, where they were procured, etc.” - translated from a comment post-Typhoon Haiyan (comment 13D)

These apprehensions about competent intervention also have implications for how Filipinos perceive taxation as a form of disaster management. The broader sentiment concerning taxation is that taxes should be used proactively in the disaster preparation stages to avoid relying on resilience (comments 3I and 12E). Most suggestions involve improved infrastructure and flood control measures (comments 24G and 38E). One portion of the discourse also emphasizes that taxes should be focused on other areas to ensure long-term and transformational change through education, livelihood, and permanent housing (comment 14G).

Despite the governance issues, the discourse also reflects pushback to enforce upward accountability. There is a general reluctance to pay taxes for disaster response due to previous experiences of government inefficiencies. Some ideas have been put forward for a wealth tax because ordinary citizens alone cannot make significant financial contributions. However, there is also an understanding of its infeasibility because many political elites also carry business interests. As such, most clamors have asked for better implementation of the existing mechanisms, specifically good governance (comment 12E).

The effect of these sentiments toward broader governance is the increased focus on bayanihan (collective cooperation) at the community level. Much like resilience, collective cooperation is also identified as an innate Filipino characteristic. These discourses focus on a community-level act involving ordinary Filipinos uplifting each other irrespective of institutional support. In this sense, elites and politicians do not engage in collective cooperation because they are detached from a “community” within the social circles of those affected.

“It is the true Filipino who does bayanihan (collective cooperation). Not the guilty politicians and the bosses.” - from a comment post-Typhoon Haiyan (comment 13F)

Similarly, the discourse also expresses that the notion of communal assistance must come from a place of discomfort. Commenters claim that the sense of support exists when the donor has limited resources and capacity. An example is the additional donation solicitation occurring during the Christmas period, which aims to get employees to provide their additional salaries and earnings toward giving back. Collective cooperation also becomes an act of mutually strengthening religious faith, with many discourses noting that giving is “being a blessing” and receiving is “being blessed.” These acts attempt to parallel certain Catholic doctrines that being “poor” yet still helping stems from faith and is being an extension of God that will be rewarded in the afterlife (comment 8F).

Subsequently, the discourse indicates that being strategic (diskarte) and trying (sikap) in fending for oneself is a sign of unity (pagkakaisa) because of the understanding that living with disaster is a universal experience. Climate disasters that have a more significant impact on the community lead to a greater sense of shared identify (kapwa), as one's identity becomes attached to those of others. As such, collective cooperation (bayanihan) is an inherent value that even strengthens with compounding disasters because the lack of institutional support lends to Filipinos being more altruistic—albeit out of necessity:

“It's like saying that paying taxes is useless. It's up to each individual and in the end, only God can be relied on. Everyone has their own savings. The government is no longer needed because all Filipinos in this calamity can stand up for each other!” - translated from a comment post-Typhoons Goni and Vamco (comment 27E)

## 4.4. Most appropriate distribution actors

Proposition #4: Providing disaster aid and relief directly to recipients is more effective than routing it through intermediary groups.

An extension of bayanihan as a form of community-centric disaster response comes from perceptions of whom material donations and other sources should be channeled. As implied from the previous propositions, the general sentiment is that Filipinos would rather wish they, themselves, provide aid directly to their intended recipients. This discourse notes that the key reasons are altruistic, as Filipinos want their donations to be utilized immediately. They also possess a fear of malpractice in the relief chain process, to varying degrees, depending on the actor.

The discourses reflect that many Filipinos would prefer to not send donations through the government. However, this does not necessarily equate to them being entirely against it. The discourse highlights some instances in which access to far-flung communities can only be accessible by government units. In this case, Filipinos should by strategic (diskarte) and determine which government agency is most competent. Within such a hierarchy, national politicians are least preferred due to fears of corruption and the delays. Local politicians are preferred, albeit donors must also exercise caution when learning if the person involved is trustworthy. In this case, donations in-kind are more favorable than cash. Finally, donations to social welfare are seen as the most effective government actor due to them facilitating on-ground operations:

“Send your donations to the right government agency. Do not be fooled by calls from politicians, now is not the time for them to exploit you. We donated food packs, water, and clothes through the Department of Social Welfare in Tacloban.” - translated from a comment post-Typhoon Rai (comment 39B)

Despite the previous findings that Filipinos’ religious devotion carries them through during disasters, comments note that Filipinos would seldom donate to the Church or faith-based organizations. This is especially true for cash donations, as posters note that the Church regularly solicits funding during religious services (comments 40A and 40E). The disdain surrounding Church-based relief is either that (1) the Church already has a substantial pool of resources from believers and should exhaust such (comments 40B, 40E, and 41I), or that (2) the Church should solely be a source of spiritual healing and that they instead are crowding the relief chain (comments 24J and 41C).

Some individuals within the discourse highlighted that sending donations through the Church will entitle them to extra blessings because the practice of Church groups handing out their aid becomes a symbol of God in action. However, this remained an outlier sentiment. These findings prove particularly interesting because there is no mistrust in the Church in carrying out relief distribution. Instead, it is knowledge of the Church's existing wealth and the role it should assume in the disaster space. People's reliance on faith does not represent their reliance on the institution prompting such faith:

“Here we are again, preachers. You have so much money, maybe you could lessen it a bit and help your members. It would be fine if the Catholic Church would not be so rich” - translated from a comment post-Typhoon Rai (comment 40C)

The discourse highlights that the private sector and non-governmental organizations are the most trustworthy actors in redistributing material donations. Its central justification is that these groups have no ulterior motive or incentive to act incompetently. Moreover, these actors were given the most leniency within the discourse, as they were seen as purely altruistic because they were not mandated to be accountable to anyone. They utilized their own resources and barely solicited. The discussion even went so far as to suggest that Filipinos should feel a greater sense of gratitude for their generosity (comment 11C).

An important feature in evaluating the best actors in the relief chain is the discourse's persistent suggestion for donation monitoring and accountability. This was most prevalent in the discussions relating to foreign aid distribution, mainly because of the aforementioned corruption concerns borne out of the mishaps from Haiyan. The discourse even suggested that foreign governments should distribute their aid themselves to avoid potential malpractice. This mirrors why Filipinos favor bypassing intermediaries entirely: to identify who benefitted from their donation tangibly (comment 45B, comment 45A).

This theme was also present to a lesser extent when scrutinizing foundations. Their supposed lower financial standing and net worth cast some doubt on whether providing cash donations will go directly to the victims or the costs of operations (i.e., salaries and overhead). In this regard, there are strong preferences for in-kind donations, with cash being a last resort when reaching the distribution actors is unattainable.

## 4.5. Prayer in disaster support

Proposition #5: At the individual level, thoughts and prayers are considered a meaningful contribution to disaster preparation and response efforts.

Given Filipinos' strong religious, prayer is a common response to climate disasters. As many Filipinos believe disasters are acts of God, whether as a test or as punishment for their wrongdoings, direct prayers are broadcast to seek repentance from God, with the eventual aim of supernatural intercession toward the typhoon before it makes landfall. For example, the comments ask for the typhoons’ weakening, shifting trajectory, or dissipating altogether. In this regard, prayer becomes an act of “miracle hunting” to directly influence natural activity (comment 20H, comment 18A).

One would also pray for their well-being alongside traditional measures (i.e., building emergency packs and evacuating). God alone will not save them, for it is an understanding that one must also utilize one's own agency to ensure their safety. In this sense, prayer is not used as a means to alter nature but instead as a complementary act, with the discourse also quoting Bible verses that concrete actions must be done for faith to take effect (comment 21B).

However, prayer's impact is seen as more pronounced as a form of spiritual aid in the immediate disaster aftermath. This discourse highlights many instances of posters broadcasting their prayers for God to provide emotional strength for affected populations, mainly through coping in moving on or exercising resilience. Prayers are also invoked for victims to realize that God has preferential treatment for them because they survived (see proposition #1) and should be used as motivation that God will support them in rebuilding their lives again. Additionally, nearly all discourses utilize “God bless” as a closing statement in their comments, which highlights a consistent hope for others to receive spiritual nourishment.

Moreover, people also use prayer as a rallying cry in how others should react in disaster response. The key examples include prayers hoping that fellow citizens can exercise collective cooperation (bayanihan), that people can unite when discussing the best courses of action, and that the government can set aside politics to focus on disaster relief. Thus, prayer becomes a powerful response mechanism with potential long-term implications as an all-encompassing act because of its supposed power to create an awakening in shifting attitudes and mindsets.

“Prayers are the best. I hope the victims move on and the hurt they feel goes away. I hope all Filipinos can help each other. I hope politicians soften their hearts and give them all the donations.” - translated from a comment post-Typhoon Haiyan (comment 15K)

Prayer also presents great feasibility as a response mechanism. The discourse emphasizes that prayer is an easy form of aid because it is non-material and does not account for accessibility issues (e.g., distance). In general, prayer is perceived equally to material aid in effectiveness due to its supernatural implications. As such, prayer can function as both a complement to material aid or as a standalone alternative, the latter being particularly true for lower-income populations who claim prayer as the sole means of helping (comment 38D, comment 15D).

## 4.6. Issues with engaging in discourse

Proposition #6: Engaging in debates or discussions about disaster response strategies may detract from the immediate goal of assisting affected populations.

While some of the other propositions highlight that Filipinos are concerned with institutional accountability, the most appropriate actors in distributing aid, and prayers, another discourse feels that engaging in discourses itself is counterproductive and a central manifestation of the Filipino phrase “actions not words” (gawa hindi salita). This indicates that those engaging in discourse utilize their energy on a “less productive” outlet instead of participating in disaster recovery efforts, which is considered the opposite of collective cooperation.

A particular group that exercises this sentiment is institutional defenders, primarily supporters of the government or those who subscribe to Filipino resilience and collective cooperation. Their comments reflect their belief that airing grievances is counterproductive because they have ulterior disingenuous motives for attacking the government's chosen action plan. In particular, they mention that highlighting problems amid disasters can lower morale for stakeholders supporting recovery and victims (comment 32E).

Within this discourse, commenters also note that “finger pointing” (comments 13E and 32D) and calls for accountability can occur after the recovery process but not during it. They claim that these other discourses crowd the content that social media users are exposed to—and with corresponding implications. An example is a claim that foreign donors, both at individual and national levels, would not be willing to donate or provide aid if they observed that fellow Filipinos were highlighting institutional incompetence and distrust (comment 14A).

Another example of crowded discourse comes from donation solicitation posts intended for specific areas. Comments included points like “our area needs help, too,” or “why is this area getting all of the attention?” Resilience and collective cooperation were meant to be mutually uplifting mindsets, yet while this discourse may not have malintent, it may imply selective assistance (comment 42C). Within this discourse, the proposed intervention is to adopt a positive mindset. However, pushback to this discourse highlights that it may build complacency and a broader acceptance of a defeatist mentality (comment 12F).

## 5. Discussion

## 5.1. General discussion

Our study contributes to the understanding of social and economic responses to climate disasters in the Philippines. As we analyze the findings through the lens of Filipino cultural values (described by Filipino Psychology) including shared identity (kapwa), fatalistic risk-taking (Bahala na), debt of gratitude (Utang na loob), collective cooperation (Bayanihan) and strategic behavior (diskarte), we develop distinct and preliminary propositions about climate disasters and values in the Philippines. We emphasize that these are context-specific insights rather than generalizable claims and acknowledge that future research would need to test these propositions across different disasters, time periods, or cultural settings to determine whether they hold beyond the context of this study.

The most prominent discourses relate to shared identity (kapwa) as a key Filipino value, whereby Filipinos' identities are intrinsically linked to one another. This shared identity creates the sense that Filipinos must answer for each other and carry their burdens. This aligns with previous studies that this shared identity plays an important role in the moral evaluation of people's actions during the eruption of the Taal volcano and other disasters [64]. As noted by other studies, social resilience in response to disasters is equated to interdependence [65], which strongly reflects the value of collective cooperation (Bayanihan). Climate disasters stimulate greater community orientation and many Filipinos engage in actions to support others, including donating, praying, and strategic behavior (diskarte) to ensure that reaches their intended recipients.

Both preparations for and responses to disasters must also be interpreted through the lens of “fatalistic risk-taking” (Bahala na). The prominent discourses about resilience directly correspond to this value, as resilience may reinforce the current disaster framework of reaction over preemptive action until existing adaptive capacities have proven to fail. This supports the view that cultural values can either strengthen or weaken motivation to prepare for disasters [66]. Previous research has shown that disaster preparedness and response are shaped by factors such as perceived severity, self-efficacy, response efficacy, behavioral intention, and perceived behavioral control [29,30,67]. Our findings suggest that such factors may also be culturally mediated. This implies that disaster preparedness and response should not only be understood in terms of individual risk perception and capability, but also through culturally embedded value systems.

Finally, accountability in disaster efforts was an important theme. For example, as highlighted by previous research, the central accountability tool for Haiyan was the Foreign Aid Transparency Hub (FAITH), which allowed the donors and the public to view the specific parties that had received aid from actors. Yet, its failure to disclose how the actors utilized such resources, its unexplained discontinuation in 2018, and a separate political discourse on aid mismanagement entailed a general reluctance toward foreign aid management [68].

Overall, our findings show that cultural value systems structure how Filipinos interpret climate disasters, assign blame, evaluate state performance, and choose between community-based versus institutional responses. These help explain persistent preferences for coping and bayanihan over anticipatory adaptation and deepen our understanding of why trust in formal governance remains fragile.

While this study accounts for these inputs in utilizing social media as its primary data source, there are several nuances present in each disaster. Palen and Hughes [69] and Zhang et al. [33] note how communication patterns are context-specific depending on the type of hazard or social media environment of a certain area's population. Moreover, Madianou (2015) highlights how social media can also perpetuate existing inequalities when low-income populations may have less visibility in the social media space due to lacking access to technology or digital illiteracy. As such, this study's discourse analysis is inherently not all-encompassing and will be treated as a representation of its sample. Further, the changes over time should also be considered. In particular, the period between Typhoon Haiyan (2013) and the more recent disasters (Goni, Vamco, Rai) was shaped by significant socio-political developments in the Philippines, including the Taal Volcano eruption and the COVID-19 lockdowns in early 2020, which heightened public sensitivity toward disaster governance. These developments contributed to the rise of a highly emotional resilience discourse. During this period, the increasing presence of organized “political trolls” [68] also shaped online dynamics, influencing amplification, suppression, or diversion of particular narratives. While we cannot empirically verify the extent of troll activity within our dataset, acknowledging these broader shifts is important for understanding how discourse may have evolved across the events included in our sample. In addition, we explicitly note the need for future research to integrate socio-political context when examining changes in post-disaster

discourse over time.

## 5.2. Policy implications

The general implication of our study is that authorities and policymakers must consider cultural value systems when designing preemptive disaster risk reduction strategies. For instance, if people perceive typhoons as supernatural phenomena or a matter of fate (propositions 1 and 5), there is a possibility that this may lead to a fatalistic mindset. Since this is connected to religious belief, disaster preparation might be strengthened through collaborations with religious groups to promote disaster preparedness by imparting messages of religious and spiritual social action alongside prayer as beneficial to oneself and one's community. Government authorities and religious groups must collaborate in information dissemination by describing preparedness not as a lack of faith, but as a form of responsibility and collective protection. Practically, this may help communicate that prayer and preparation can coexist, which would allow communities to take proactive measures before disasters occur.

Given the importance of cooperation (bayanihan) and shared identity (kapwa) in Filipino culture, community-based responses should be participatory to improve disaster and science communication in climate adaptation efforts. Community resilience can be strengthened by reinforcing the baranggay system, the basic unit of government in the Philippines, as the most equipped on-the-ground actor for improving disaster management. Local government units (LGUs) must conduct consultations and capacitate baranggays by providing climate disaster preparedness-related training, community evacuation drills, neighborhood-based early warning systems, such as announcement or radio systems, particularly in areas without mobile and internet connection, and volunteer disaster response teams. This is particularly important in the country because many municipalities and cities cover large areas, and LGUs often lack the capacity to reach every community.

Moreover, national and local government actors should aim for transparent accountability mechanisms, particularly due to skepticism related to taxation and public disaster funds. For instance, there should be a clear and well-defined list of people who receive disaster funds and relief goods. Consultations should also be conducted before and after disaster response efforts. In addition, transparency should go beyond simply posting budgets on bulletin boards or online before and after disasters. It should involve complete transparency through public meetings or other forms of information dissemination. More specifically, the language used in these reports must be understandable to the public. This may improve institutional trust and allow Filipinos to better understand the context and judgment needed to determine the extent to which they should enact community-based responses. It may also enable a healthier discursive environment that is issue-based and goal-centric at heart.

## 5.3. Limitations

There are limitations to be considered. First, one limitation is related to Facebook as a data source. Facebook's in-site search function allows basic filtering, including date/s posted, keywords, and public versus private post accessibility. However, it lacks advanced filtering options that would have greatly contributed to expediting the data-gathering process. A feature that would have particularly benefited would be the ability to filter through engagement statistics to work with the objectively most prominent discourses. In addition, Facebook only allows users to access a limited number of posts per search query before it stops searching. Second, the lack of social media discourse on particular sentiments that were otherwise included in the literature review. Examples include Field's [15] findings on “return to social” normalcy interventions, Bankoff's [12] insight on communities not evacuating in complete confidence of divine intervention, or any sentiment toward being unable or even hostile to aiding others. Not inductively finding such on social media may result from (1) fears of perceived backlash when broadcasting antisocial behavior, (2) predominantly news sources as the data source bringing solely “mainstream” ideas, (3) the risk of compromising one's existing social ties, or (4) directly vulnerable populations not being present or posting on social media during disaster situations. Nevertheless, the strength of the method lies not in the size or representativeness of the sample, but rather in its ability to provide rich insights into how people construct meaning and express experiences through language.

## 6. Conclusion

Culture can play a decisive role in how individuals and institutions manage climate disasters, especially in the Philippines. However, the policy framework focuses on coping and recovery over preparedness and adaptation, which has faced criticism. Given the country's vulnerability to climate disasters, we examine the role of cultural value systems in discourses about disaster management. We conduct a discourse analysis using social media comments after four major typhoons from 2013 to 2021. Based on our analysis of 306 comments, we propose six preliminary propositions related to attitudes toward climate change and disasters (i) being influenced by supernatural interpretations, (ii) self-reliance being linked to institutional complacency in adaptation, (iii) lacking trust in authority presenting negative perceptions towards taxation and an inclination for community-based response, (iv) donations preferably being coursed directly to recipients with a hierarchy of preferences for intermediary actors, (v) prayer as an effective and cost-efficient non-material form of aid, and (vi) engaging in discourse as a detraction from the immediate need to help. By identifying how cultural value systems inform post-disaster discourse, we offer a framework for understanding the persistence of recovery-focused disaster governance in the Philippines. We recommend that future studies and behavioral interventions account for these cultural perceptions of climate disasters in improving disaster management.

Comments on this post are more intellectual. Not necessarily on practical solutions. More on theorizing the concept of resilience.

I dunno maybe I&#x27;m wrong but if people wanted they could make things happen to achieve it: good government, better lives, better futures but I don&#x27;t see any sign that we&#x27;ve had enough bullshit from leaders promising to be the Superman to lead us out of our personal shitholes, fix our economy while safeguarding our freedom and protecting the future for our children. So until I see any clear sign that us Filipinos are ready to take off our blinders, quit waiting for self-proclaimed national saviors and take on the responsibility of attaining change instead of waiting for institutional change (never going to happen) - we will remain like survivors on lifeboat drifting rudderless and without any sense of where we are or where we&#x27;re headed.</td></tr></table>

General post about privillaged people as the only ones who can glorify “resillience” due to their dettached view from a place of comfort, while those affected cannot do the same. Poster says that Filipino “resilience” is an excuse for a lack of foresight from the government's end - saying that good governance can be controlled by the citizenry, particularly in urban planning and utilizing media for disaster communications. Private sector and citizen efforts aren't enough.

It probably entails that doing bayanihan also entails that one is within a place of discomfort as well??</td></tr><tr><td>13G</td><td>Call to extend what would have been given for Christmas to be extended toward donation/relief instead. Could point to how the Filipino Christmas spirit is larger than that of most countries, and how most disasters fall in that range due to the typhoon season.</td></tr><tr><td>17F</td><td>Bahanihan as hypocritical when people in government preaching it are still prone to corruption. It no longer becomes a “communal” thing when not the “entire” community isn&#x27;t participating</td></tr><tr><td>17H</td><td>Nothing will get past the PH kung “magsama-sama” tayo (unity and togetherness)</td></tr><tr><td>21B</td><td>Prayer for God + a word of advice for how survivors should evacuate. Justification that prayer and other forms of discourse not be mutually exclusive (continued on next page)</td></tr></table>

| Providing | disaster aid and relief directly to recipients is more effective than routing it through intermediary organizations. |
